items.title: Noah’s Ark Researcher Reveals Stunning New Detail About Wood Discovered at the Site
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

There’s yet another major development surrounding Noah’s Ark. Wood uncovered at a site some believe houses the famed vessel’s remains has officially been dated to 4,300 years ago, though many questions persist.

Andrew Jones, founder of Noah’s Ark Scans, a group managing the dig at the site, told CBN News that researchers collected two plastic bags worth of “burned-looking wood samples.” Researchers sent two samples for testing, with one going through a fast-track process in Florida.

“We got the results back on Nov. 18,” Jones said. “The wood samples from this location on the Durupinar … boat site are dating around 4,300 years old.”

Some biblical chronologies would align with this timing, though the Septuagint would place it earlier. Jones said he’s aware of the debate on timing, but is not concerned about those factors at the moment.

“We’re just reporting the results of what we’ve done so far,” he said. “Now we have two more labs that are going to report the results over the next couple months. One’s a lab in Turkey — a Turkish government facility — and then the other one is a lab in Switzerland.”

These results should give additional information that will help to frame and contextualize the wood findings. Jones said one of the lead researchers also plans to ask a Turkish lab to “help determine the type of species, the type of wood it is, if possible.”

Jones said, though he has been confident about the site, he is taking research and results one step at a time, taking great care to come to science-based conclusions.

“We know there’s a worldwide interest in this project,” Jones said. “And so we said, ‘Hey, this is what the wood showed. … We don’t know what the other two labs will show.'”

He continued, “So we’re just doing step-by-step.”

Some critics have long alleged the boat-shape structure underground is composed of stone and not wood, which has still been undetermined. Regardless, the discovery of wood at the site has been shocking to some who ponder whether the wood could be some sort of evidence for remnants from the biblical flood.

“These lines of evidence pointing to this being not just a natural ship shape there, but the buried decayed remains of the ark — this is another line of evidence that we never had before that was recently discovered and now tested by independent lab,” Jones said. “We have more tests coming up that’s pointing to whatever’s in there dating to the time of the flood.”

He added, “From there, people can debate the Carbon-14 dates from a creationist standpoint. They can debate, if it was post-flood, it got in there somehow.”

Researchers will also explore evidence of potential pitch on the wood or another such coating.

Jones encouraged people to pray for the project.

“We just ask that God give everybody wisdom in navigating these issues, and the scientific method, and making sure if it is really Noah’s Ark,” he said.

items.title: Faith Directly Tied to Greater Quality of Life in Seniors
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A new survey is revealing older adults who are religious enjoy a better quality of life than those who don’t believe in God.

Researchers from the University of Padua in Italy combed through studies of more than 5,600 adults over 60 years old. In all, the data showed people who have made faith a routine part of their lives reported greater benefits than those who only turn to God in difficult times or not at all, CNN reported.

“Across the studies we pooled, older adults who were more religious or spiritual reported higher life satisfaction and better quality of life,” said lead author Sohail Akhtar. “The link was moderate in size, but it was consistent enough to suggest that spiritual life deserves a place in how we support healthy aging.”

Listen to the latest episode of the “Quick Start” podcast

Of the studies, 10 were conducted in Asia, seven in America, three in Europe, and one in Africa. They consisted of participants ranging in ages from 60 to 104 and included 2,503 women, 1,561 men, and 1,600 people whose sex was not reported.

The link to greater satisfaction was highest in Asia, followed by Africa, then America.

Analysts for the study said that, in addition to improving practitioners’ wellbeing, faith “can provide social interaction, emotional support, and cognitive stimulation, which aids life satisfaction and even mortality.”

“This meta-analysis once again points to the importance of spirituality and religiosity in providing resources for good quality of life in later life,” Paul Higgs, professor of sociology of aging at the University of London, told CNN. “It is interesting that this is strongest in Asia and Africa, continents where religion and spirituality are still important aspects of social and cultural life.”

The Bible is full of passages encouraging us to turn to God because He is a wellspring of wisdom, which He gives us freely when we ask (James 1:5) and fills us with joy and peace when we trust Him (Romans 15:13).

items.title: A Record 25.2 Million Young Adults Won’t Be Traveling Home for Thanksgiving Because They Already Live There
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: At some point this week, somebody at a Thanksgiving table is going to get asked when they’re finally moving out. If that somebody is you, here’s a number to bring to dinner. A record 25.2 million Americans ages 18 to 34 lived with their parents in 2025, according to a new report from Realtor.com. Th
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

At some point this week, somebody at a Thanksgiving table is going to get asked when they’re finally moving out. If that somebody is you, here’s a number to bring to dinner.

A record 25.2 million Americans ages 18 to 34 lived with their parents in 2025, according to a new report from Realtor.com. That’s 33%, about one in three young adults, just under the 2020 pandemic peak of 33.6%.

Realtor.com chief economist Danielle Hale said a growing number of young adults “don’t have far to travel because they’re already living with mom or dad, which says a lot about housing affordability and opportunity.”

Where you live makes a big difference. New York leads the country, with 41.3% of young adults living with their parents. Philadelphia and Miami come next at 38.6%, followed by Baltimore at 38.5% and Houston at 38.2%. In Los Angeles, more than one in five adults ages 30 to 34 live at home, nearly twice the national rate for that age group.

The fastest growth is in places that used to be easier to launch from. Las Vegas jumped 4.4 percentage points from the pandemic years to 31.3%, after home prices there rose 62.7% since 2019. San Francisco and San Jose climbed 4.3 and 3.9 points. In the South, the share has risen from 26.6% in 2000 to 32.3%, and the Midwest just hit a record 14.8% among 25- to 34-year-olds.

“The pattern of young adults at home has spread beyond the most expensive markets,” Hale said, “with the share rising most in parts of the South and West, including some that have traditionally supported an earlier launch.”

The at-home crowd is also getting older. Most are 18 to 24, but 25- to 34-year-olds make up a growing share, reaching 32.6% of young adults living with parents in the West.

So the math has changed, even if your aunt’s questions haven’t. Living at home at 27 says a lot more about rent than about you.

Hale’s bigger worry is what the delay costs. “As young people adapt to high housing costs, they are delaying homeownership and the wealth creation that comes with it,” she said.

For now, the commute to Thanksgiving is a walk down the hall. Pass the rolls. You know where they are.

items.title: If It Die: Profound Suffering Serves as a Catalyst
items.author: Gary Saul Morson
items.summary:
Gary Saul Morson

For those who discover God, the soul, or the afterlife, what changes them is not rational demonstration but searing experience, especially the experience of suffering.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Gary Saul Morson

This article is featured in Issue XXIX: “Literature” of the Word on Fire Institute’s quarterly journal, Evangelization & Culture.

. . .

Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.

—John 12:24 KJV

Has anyone ever found faith by reading a philosophical argument for God’s existence? All those arguments of medieval and Age of Reason philosophers—aren’t they beside the point? After all, if there were such a thing as faith based on rational argument, would it not be forever vulnerable to some new counterargument? If so, then perhaps the role of rational argument is not to prove that God exists but to show that it is far from certain that he does not exist. Philosophy can, at best, make room for faith achieved some other way.

That is what one hero of Tolstoy’s War and Peace, Prince Andrei, tells the other, his friend Pierre. When Pierre asks what arguments have changed his mind, Andrei answers that arguments, such as those Pierre has been paraphrasing, are beside the point. What has changed Andrei is something far deeper: the experience of his wife’s death and the agonizing realization that he can never make up for the wrongs he did to her. “All I say is that it is not arguments that persuade one of the necessity of a future life,” he confesses, “but this: when in life you go hand in hand with someone, and suddenly that person vanishes there, into nowhere, and you are left facing that abyss, looking down into it. . . . And I did look into it.”

Profound suffering serves as a catalyst. This insight applies to many heroes of Russian literature who discover God, the soul, or the afterlife. What changes them is not rational demonstration but searing experience, especially the experience of suffering. Shaken to the depths, these heroes discover that they do not really believe what they thought they believed. For Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn and other Gulag prisoners, cruelty and suffering beyond anything they had imagined possible make them reflect. Faced with extreme evil, they cannot doubt that morality has a fundamental basis in the nature of things. They discover the soul when it is pierced to the core. As there are no atheists in foxholes, there are no relativists in the Gulag.

Even nonbelievers who experienced Stalin’s labor camps testify that when faced with the choice between someone else’s life and their own well-being, Communist atheists always behaved selfishly. The only ones who consistently did not were the believers in something higher than mere existence and more important than their own lives. Sometimes it is not prison but other traumatic experiences that bring real people and fictional characters to God—such as the guilt and regret that has stricken Prince Andrei. 

In Dostoevsky’s great Christian novel The Brothers Karamazov, suffering offers an opportunity for faith, but does not ensure it. As with divine grace, one must respond in the right way. Dostoevsky chose for the novel’s epigraph John 12:24: “Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (KJV). By this he meant profound suffering may occasion spiritual rebirth, but only if we allow it to do so. 

One of the Karamazov brothers, Dmitri, endures the agonizing experience of arrest for a crime he did not commit, and is spiritually reborn. Another, Ivan, suffers fruitlessly. 

Ivan discovers that he has not only desired the death of his sadistic father but has also unwittingly enabled it. Without quite knowing it, he has arranged for his villainous illegitimate half brother, Smerdyakov, to murder the old man. Ivan also realizes that he could have known, but avoided doing so just because he wanted the crime to happen “against his will.” Smerdyakov, who hates his legitimate brothers for not accepting him, leads Ivan to the recognition of his guilt, not all at once but step-by-step, in three long conversations, so as to maximize the agony of self-examination. This experience could be the occasion for Ivan’s spiritual rebirth, and it almost is, but unlike Dmitri, Ivan once again allows himself not to do what he should: go immediately to the prosecutor to tell him what he knows. 

Visiting Dmitri on the eve of his trial, the third Karamazov brother, the pious Alyosha, finds him in despair—not because he anticipates a conviction but because of a philosophical conversation with the atheist intellectual Rakitin. The poorly educated Dmitri struggles comically to paraphrase what he has heard:

Imagine: inside, in the nerves, in the head—that is, these nerves are there in the brain . . . (damn them!) there are sort of little tails, the little tails of these nerves, and as soon as they begin quivering . . . that is, you see, I look at something with my eyes and then they begin quivering, those little tails . . . and when they quiver, then an image appears . . . it doesn’t appear at once, but an instant, a second, passes . . . and then something like a moment appears; that is, not a moment—devil take the moment!—but an image; that is, an object, or an action, damn it! That’s why I see and then think, because of those tails, not at all because I’ve got a soul, and that I am some sort of image and likeness. All that is nonsense! Rakitin explained it all to me yesterday, brother, and it simply bowled me over. It’s magnificent, Alyosha, this science!

Like other progressive intellectuals of the day, Rakitin expects that this discovery will lead to a “new man” creating a better world. Dmitri’s reaction is entirely different: “I am sorry to lose God,” he tells Alyosha. “It’s chemistry, brother, chemistry! There’s no help for it, your reverence, you must make way for chemistry.”

Today we call the idea that so upsets Dmitri the neurological theory of consciousness. Readers are often surprised to discover that what they take to be a recent discovery was already a commonplace in late-nineteenth-century Russia. It was first expressed by the neurophysiologist Ivan Sechenov—better remembered as the teacher of Ivan Pavlov—in an 1862 article entitled “Reflexes of the Brain.” According to Sechenov, consciousness and free choice are nothing but brain activity, fundamentally no different from the contracting of our pupils in bright light. To be sure, we may have the sensation of choosing our actions, but that sensation is itself as automatic and as governed by brain activity as any other reflex.

For Dostoevsky and many others, Sechenov’s denial of anything like a soul, along with other popular ideas denying the existence of God, carried disturbing implications for human morality. If there is no God, and nothing exists beyond the material world, where does morality come from? What is it based on? Could it possibly be nothing more than variable social convention? That is, is goodness entirely relative—or as Pascal famously remarked: “Three degrees of latitude upset the whole of jurisprudence. . . it is a funny sort of justice whose limits are marked by a river; true on one side of the Pyrenees, false on the other.” Dmitri poses the question in his own frenetic way: “But after all, what is goodness? . . . Goodness is one thing with me and another with a Chinaman, so it’s a relative thing. Or isn’t it? Is it not relative? A treacherous question! You won’t laugh if I tell you it’s kept me awake two nights. I only wonder now how people can live and think nothing about it.” 

This question leaves Dmitri sleepless because he recognizes, as Rakitin does not, that if morality is entirely relative, literally anything can be justified, which in turn means that sooner or later anything, no matter how awful, is likely to take place. One reason that Dostoevsky, and only Dostoevsky, foresaw the horrors we call totalitarianism is that he recognized where the death of faith could lead. He also recognized that once a person considers morality mere convention, fundamentally no different from using the proper hand to hold one’s fork or driving on the correct side of the road, he is bound to see that “all is permitted.” Let the common herd follow moral laws as if they had some firm objective basis, such a person is bound to think; an educated person aware of the sheer arbitrariness of right and wrong is morally free to commit crimes and will eventually do so if he can be sure of not being caught. The hero of Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment argues himself into murder in just this way. 

I have known people who, like some of Dostoevsky’s characters and many of his contemporaries, dismiss the terrible consequences of materialism and relativism as fantastic. They have no desire to kill or rob anyone, they affirm. Perhaps not, Dostoevsky answered such claims, but only because sheer habit allows old moral behavior to persist a while by sheer inertia even when the basis for it has been lost. Over time, those habits weaken. That is why Dostoevsky predicted that even when some causes of crime, such as poverty and inequality, are diminished, crime will remain or even increase because something far more potent has disappeared: the conviction that, regardless of consequences, some things are simply, and objectively, just plain wrong.

Morality maintained by inertia is bound to prove inadequate when extraordinary circumstances test it. The comfortable can entertain any belief without disturbing their dinner, but when really put to the test, they are likely to fail.

The moral implications of atheism have made Ivan Karamazov dissatisfied with it. He is torn by a contradiction. On the one hand, as a student of natural science, he knows, just knows, that people are only material objects and that goodness is purely conventional. Or as one Dostoevsky character expresses the point, crime is not a crime. On the other hand, Ivan is convinced, just as certainly, that some things—like heinous cruelty to children—are incontestably wrong. He has even assembled from the Russian press a catalogue of horrific child abuse cases. Ivan’s conviction is so strong, he tells Alyosha, that he would not change it even if he knew it was mistaken. 

Ivan’s key moment occurs when Smerdyakov convinces him of his responsibility for his father’s murder and for the self-deception leading to it. On the way to his third conversation with Smerdyakov, Ivan is in a foul mood because he already senses, though he does not fully realize, the terrible truth. When a drunken peasant bumps into him, Ivan angrily pushes him away. The peasant falls on the bitterly cold ground and lies there moaning. “He will be frozen,” thinks Ivan, and passes on. 

When Ivan returns from the fateful conversation, everything changes. Now that he acknowledges his complicity in parricide, he takes the trouble to have the peasant cared for and “a liberal hand for the expenses.” The incident unmistakably alludes to the story of the Good Samaritan, with Ivan playing both roles: first the priest who “passed by on the other side” and then the Samaritan who brings him to the inn and pays his expenses (Luke 10:25–37). 

Ivan’s “critical moment” (to use Dostoevsky’s phrase) has arrived. He realizes that he should immediately follow up his good deed by going to the prosecutor and telling him everything he knows. He must confess his own criminality without delay. But, assuring himself he can always do the right thing tomorrow, he postpones doing so—that is, he repeats the same mistake he made when he postponed examining his conscience.

When Ivan returns to his lodging, he encounters the devil in what Dostoevsky’s skeptical narrator calls a nightmare but what Ivan (correctly?) regards as reality. Either way, the devil mocks him for his deferred “noble resolution” to confess. By morning, Ivan is insane. Choosing not to choose, resolving but not doing, and postponing what must be done right away, he loses his soul along with his mind.

Dmitri makes the opposite choice. What he, facing condemnation to decades of hard labor in Siberian mines, cares about most is losing his faith in God. As he tells Alyosha, when he was locked up during the preliminary investigation, “He had a strange dream, utterly out of keeping with the place and the time,” a hint that it might come from a sacred source. 

Dmitri dreamed that while driving across the steppe, he encountered a village of destitute peasants who had lost everything in a fire and were enduring hunger in the bitter cold. The peasant women were

all thin and wan . . . especially one at the edge, a tall, bony woman, who looked forty, but might have been only twenty, with a long thin face. And in her arms was a little baby crying. And her breasts seemed so dried up that there was not a drop of milk in them. And the child cried and cried, and held out its little bare arms, with its fists blue from cold.

When Dmitri asks why the child is crying, the coachman offers the obvious answer that the “babe” (as he tenderly calls it) weeps because it is cold and hungry. But that is not what Dmitri is asking: He wants to know why anyone suffers, why the steppe is barren, why there is evil in the world, why people do not sing songs of joy. “And he felt that, though his questions were unreasonable and senseless, yet he wanted to ask just that.” 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Dmitri’s unanswerable question arises from pity “such as he had never known before, . . . that he wanted to do something for them all, so that the babe should weep no more, so that . . . no one should shed tears again from that moment, and he wanted to do it at once, at once, regardless of all obstacles, with all the recklessness of the Karamazovs.” 

Dmitri tells Alyosha that his riotous behavior, which has gotten him into such trouble, must have resulted from the feeling expressed in his dream of the babe. “It was perhaps just because ideas I did not understand were surging up in me, that I used to drink and fight and rage. I was trying to stifle them in myself,” but didn’t know it. Suffering has allowed Dmitri to discover the depths of his soul, and he joyously reports that “a new man has risen up in me. He was hidden in me, but would never have come to the surface, if it hadn’t been for this blow from heaven.” 

Dmitri explains that his only fear is that his revived faith will dissipate. If it does not, then he can brave any punishment. Even if he is sentenced to dig for years in underground mines, he can still find and love another human heart. He is sure his dream was not just brain activity but something deeply meaningful. “Why was it I dreamed of that ‘babe’ at such a moment?” he asks. It was because the dream “was a sign to me. It’s for the babe I’m going [to the mines]. Because we are all responsible for all.” So long as people have faith, Dmitri continues, then, even in chains, even in “great sorrow, we shall rise again to joy . . . for God gives joy. . . . Ah, man should be dissolved in prayer!” 

Rakitin, he allows, would laugh at such a feeling. People like him are doing away with God, Dmitri continues, but “if they drive God from the earth, we shall shelter Him underground. . . . And then we men underground will sing from the bowels of the earth a glorious hymn to God, with Whom is joy. . . . I love Him!”

Ivan and Dmitri represent opposing responses to suffering and the insights it makes possible. One brother is like the corn of wheat that abides alone. The other resembles the one that falls into the ground and dies, bringing forth much fruit.

items.title: The Heart of Culture Is Worship: Recovering Our Catholic and Classical Tradition
items.author: Daniel Fitzpatrick
items.summary:
Daniel Fitzpatrick

If the kind of education we provide is to be sufficient to ensure that we and our children are able to enjoy the kind of life we desire for them, it is critical that we allow the tradition to live in us.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Daniel Fitzpatrick

Tertullian, the North African theologian of the second and third centuries, famously asked, “What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?” That is, at the most basic level, what can reason offer in light of Christ’s cross and resurrection? What can philosophy say to Golgotha? What cave can prompt more authentic discovery of the truth than the empty tomb of Christ? The questions are good ones to ask ourselves, particularly for those committed to evangelizing in our own parishes, schools, and homes.

So I ask, what has Athens to do with Covington—the city in Louisiana which I now call home—or with any other place laboring along under the haunting of the cross? What can the tradition of Western learning, with its intense study of Latin, its love of Homer, its grammar and logic and rhetoric, its geometry and astronomy, its arithmetic and music, add to our experience of the Gospel? And how can the Gospel, the parables, the apocalyptic warnings, the miracles, translate our particular culture to the plane of the eternal?

Culture is the central matter here. And while culture incorporates all aspects of human life, from food and language and art to dress and design and gestures, the heart of culture is worship. Whatever we worship, whether we understand that worship as such or not, becomes the heart of our culture. A society that worships God does things like build cathedrals and compose Divine Comedies and Summae Theologicae. A society that worships Baal sacrifices its infants. Where do we find the marks of worship today? What are the defining features of our culture? Are they the Super Bowl, the Eras tour, the golden arches of McDonald’s? The screens and the data centers and the social media feeds? Culture is a question of value: a question of what a man, a family, or a city will stake their life on.

In thinking of culture, as of so many other things, we can do worse than to start with the Greeks. There are a number of Greek words connected with culture, but two are of particular interest for us: paideia and nomos. Paideia essentially means education. It’s where we get our words pedagogue, pedagogy, and so on. In a literal sense, paideia means “childing,” the total cultural formation of children that shapes them according to that culture’s dominant values. 

Among the Greeks, several visions of paideia emerged, but perhaps the two which have most firmly impressed our imagination are the Athenian and the Spartan. Athenian paideia prized the musical soul in the beautiful body. In the palestra and the gymnasium, by wrestling and gymnastics, through debate and the practice of the flute and the lyre, above all in the verses of Homer, Athenians pursued kalokagathia, that lovely nobility that breaks forth in the structure of the Parthenon and the tragedies of Aeschylus, the dialogues of Plato and sculptures of Phidias. In Athens, we find an impulse toward the harmony of the human and divine.

The Spartans, if less influential on our art and philosophy, nonetheless live in our cultural imagination as the archetypal warriors. Their paideia looks less to the perfection of the individual than to the security of the state. Their child is taken early from his family. He lives communally, is taught to bear cold and hunger, trained to take what he can and not to be caught. Plutarch recounts the story of a Spartan boy who, having stolen a fox and concealed it within his tunic, allows the fox to rip out his innards rather than be detected. This is the kind of boy who grows up to star in 300—if, that is, a fox hasn’t eaten his intestines. 

Athenian and Spartan paideia were intimately connected with each people’s way of life. The Athenians lived democratically, established themselves commercially at sea, developed drama and sculpture and architecture to such heights as have scarcely been equalled in the millennia since. The Spartans lived under a pair of kings, training for war yet rarely going on campaign due to the danger of a helot rebellion. And their lives were rather, well, Spartan—much less concerned with the arts and other cultural trappings than the Athenians. 

These cultures were regularly in tension with each other, a tension which exploded ultimately in the Peloponnesian War. The tide of that conflict, which was in some sense a world war unto itself, swept one way and then the other. Ultimately, though, the Spartans emerged victorious. But their hegemony would be brief, and an exhausted Greece would before long fall under the power of Macedon, first under Philip II, and finally under his son, Alexander the Great.

Now, it’s worth remembering that no culture—save that of Christ’s Church—will endure forever. Egypt, Greece, Rome, the Incas, the Aztecs, the British, all the world’s powers come eventually to crumble and fade. (The sun never sets on your nostalgia, goes a line from Dana Gioia that we would‑be culturists ought to keep in mind.) Even America will one day be no more, and that is largely because no amount of regret or recrimination can unmake or even amend the fall. Only Christ’s cross and resurrection can do that, and only the bark of Peter can abide safely on the flood of grace that will wash the world till the end of time. 

The question for us, then, is how to secure our culture. If the kind of education we provide is to be sufficient to ensure that we and our children are able to enjoy the kind of life we desire for them, it is critical that we allow the tradition to live in us. We stand in need of a true renaissance, a rebirth, for indeed the particular challenge of our time is that much of the tradition has not simply gone dormant, has not simply retreated, but has effectively died. Who among us has a real working knowledge of Latin? Who can define accurately what it means to beg the question? To commit the argumentum ad verecundiam fallacy? The false dilemma? Who can give proper definitions in the Aristotelian tradition, translate an argument into a syllogism, a syllogism into an enthymeme? These are the kinds of questions Dorothy Sayers raises in her 1947 address, “The Lost Tools of Learning.” Have the seventy-nine years since witnessed a resurgence in such knowledge of the classical tradition? Or have they rather not seen a more and more precipitous decline in our capacities for language such that it often feels as though contemporary discourse, even if conducted in the same tongue, is just so much barbaric shouting back and forth, like Fortunato and Montresor in Poe’s “The Cask of Amontillado,” two men screaming at each other in the dark across a wall well on its way to completion?

What, then, of our paideia? What kind of culture should we seek to form if we want our way of life to endure?

To answer the question, we ought first to ask what sort of people we want our education to form. What should the aim of a Catholic education be? We ought to hope in the first place that our children will have been formed by examples of sanctity, so they too can become saints. There is, after all, only one ultimate failure in human life, as Leon Bloy put it: not to have been a saint. 

The saint is the one who responds to God’s love moment by moment in the concrete circumstances of life. And while holiness is, in the end, a matter of grace, we can at least begin at school and at home to share with our students the sacramental life of the Church and her theological and philosophical traditions, the example of the lives of the saints, the wisdom of the bark of Peter that has ridden out all the storms of these two millennia. 

We can recognize, too, that the Church has made the classical tradition her own by a long and still ongoing rapprochement evident in the works of Tertullian and Origen, Jerome and Augustine, Basil and More and Aquinas, and that that tradition, faithfully pursued, supplies some of the best armor against the threats of the world. Who has not seen the sons and daughters of good Catholic families turned from faith by the cares and arguments of society? Who has not seen a faithful child turned a scornful and sullen adult? And while, again, much depends on the unseen powers at work in the world and in our hearts, the merciful flood of grace and the cunning of evil, our children need, as Dorothy Sayers puts it, armor. They need to be able to recognize falsehood when they see it on television or TikTok or Instagram, and not only to recognize it as false but to be able to say why. At present, so many of them are sent into the world without the tools of grammar, logic, and rhetoric, which can not only supply them defenses against the world’s falsehoods and fallacious arguments, but also serve as weapons for the good as tools for persuasion. The classical tradition seeks to produce the vir bonus dicendi peritus, the good person capable of persuasion. We want not an Alcibiades but an Augustine, not a Gorgias but a Gregory. We need men and women who can recognize the good, do it themselves, and persuade others to do so too. 

Hence the critical importance of an education that is truly classical, an education that founds itself on the arts of language. When we speak of grammar and logic and rhetoric in the classical sense, we mean not simply the rules of syntax and punctuation or of general clear thinking or of obfuscating the truth to win an argument. We mean rather coming to understand the very nature of language and thought and communication as the human person’s way of interfacing with the created order, an order brought about through the Logos, the Word who fashions the grammar and logic of all that is and allows those things to speak so persuasively to the soul. Yet knowing the rules of language is only part of the battle. We need our students to be formed for virtue, and while reading good books does not make people virtuous, literature provides students with an imaginative theater of moral action which can, at secondhand, form them for virtue. Who can read The Old Man and the Sea without learning something about magnanimity and endurance? Who can take up War and Peace without meditating on patience and prudence? Who can hear A Tale of Two Cities without being shifted slightly toward temperance and authentic empathy?

While the classical tradition can arm children against the wiles of the prince of this world and equip them to some extent for moral action, the Catholic tradition provides a grounding to ensure that the powers of oratory are properly directed. Jerusalem, in the end, does not need Athens. One can be a saint without ever having set down a syllogism or memorized a word of Vergil. But thank God that he has given us Athens too.

Athens and Sparta both came to their ends. As did Macedon. As did Rome. As do they all. Some have fallen through failures of culture, others by war, still others by simple foolishness. It’s possible that even a good society can go down into the dust through the most moronic devices. Friends of Narnia will recall that the end of that world comes about through the chicanery of an ape and a donkey in a lion skin. In Lewis’s imagination, the midsummer night’s dream becomes a nightmare, faerie becomes the province of fear. Unlike the lovers of Shakespeare’s Athens, the king and good talking beasts find in the woods no green world reenchantments; with the thickets of custom cut down, they find the very devil rounding on them, and with them and Peter and Lucy and Edmund, we readers can only watch as the universe we’ve come to love is swept away.

One day our world, too, the world to which, for all its foolishness, love still calls us, will be gathered up and shaken free of its grossness and made one with the heavenly realm where even now Christ and his Mother await us in bodily blessedness. We cannot make heaven on earth. But we can teach our children—and ourselves—to see the presence of heaven in every earthly thing, even in language and the fabric of being that it represents. We can teach them to see the difference between true speech and false speech. We can teach them to use their words in harmony with the Word, such that their lives on earth can become the cover and title to the story which has no end, where every chapter is better than the one before.
